items.text: Ending ageing, so that people can stay healthy for centuries, should be one of medicine's main goals.
items.rationale: Life-extension advocates and transhumanists endorse; bioconservatives see ageing as part of a good human life. Works in both frames: ideal priority vs. how medicine is actually aimed today.

items.text: It is good for healthy people to use safe drugs or implants that sharpen their memory and focus.
items.rationale: Pro-enhancement liberals and transhumanists endorse; therapy-only bioconservatives (Sandel, Kass) reject even safe enhancement. 'Safe' keeps it about enhancement itself, not risk.

items.text: If a brain-computer link proves safe in trials, healthy people who want one should be able to get one.
items.note: A brain-computer link is a device that connects the brain directly to a computer.
items.rationale: Condition removes the safety objection, favouring the Transhumanist pole; bioconservatives object on grounds of human integrity. Frames can split on trust in real-world trials.

items.text: Editing the genes of future children to give them greater abilities, such as higher intelligence, is acceptable.
items.rationale: Liberal eugenicists and transhumanists (Savulescu, Harris) endorse; strong claim because it goes beyond disease prevention. Readable as a principle in both frames.

items.text: If editing an embryo's genes can prevent a serious inherited disease, parents should be free to choose it.
items.rationale: Condition (clear medical benefit) favours the Transhumanist pole; religious and precautionary bioconservatives still reject embryo editing. Here-and-now answers may differ with trust in local regulators and clinics.

items.text: Building artificial intelligence that is smarter than humans at everything is a goal worth pursuing.
items.rationale: Accelerationists and AI optimists endorse; AI-restraint advocates of left, right and religious stripes reject. Ideal vs. here-and-now can split on trust in who is actually building it.

items.text: If an AI system makes fewer mistakes than human doctors, its diagnosis should be followed over theirs.
items.rationale: Condition (proven accuracy) favours the Transhumanist pole; bioconservatives value human judgement and accountability in care. Avoids political decision-making to stay off the dem axis.

items.text: Ageing and death are natural limits that people should accept, not problems for technology to solve.
items.rationale: Mirror of tec-01. Kass-style bioconservatives and many religious and traditional thinkers endorse; life-extension advocates reject. Value claim, meaningful in both frames.

items.text: Medicine should focus on healing the sick, not on making healthy people better than normal.
items.rationale: Mirror of tec-02: the therapy/enhancement line that bioconservatives defend and transhumanists reject. Agent-neutral; applies to any medical system.

items.text: If a drug or implant that boosts healthy minds has unknown long-term effects, it should be kept off the market.
items.rationale: Precautionary condition favours the Bioconservative pole; transhumanists' proactionary view accepts unknown risk for consenting adults. Frames can split on trust in real product oversight.

items.text: Editing the genes that people pass on to their children should be off-limits, whatever the purpose.
items.note: This means edits to eggs, sperm or embryos that would be inherited, not treatments that affect only one patient.
items.rationale: Mirror of tec-04: categorical germline ban held by religious bioconservatives, Habermas-style critics and some disability advocates. 'Whatever the purpose' matches level 3.

items.text: If harm to future generations cannot be ruled out, editing human embryos should be off-limits.
items.rationale: Precautionary condition favours the Bioconservative pole; transhumanists reject a rule-out standard as one no technology meets. Mirror of tec-05.

items.text: Developing artificial intelligence that could become smarter than humans should be off-limits.
items.rationale: Mirror of tec-06. AI-pause advocates, religious humanists and techno-sceptics endorse; accelerationists reject. Answerable without naming any enforcer.

items.text: If nobody can explain how an AI system reaches its decisions, it should be kept out of roles like judging, hiring or medical care.
items.rationale: Condition (opacity) favours the Bioconservative pole; AI optimists accept opaque systems that perform well. Pairs with tec-07; frames can split on how opaque deployed systems really are.
